The engine reads the number as the reporting currency whatever the unit says, so a dollar figure left here reads as CHF and overstates the product by the exchange rate.
column12: Scale for a reader: the same file shows 4,382,840.5 dosage units over those 438 beneficiaries, 10,007 units or 5,003 mg each. At the labelled maintenance dose of 1.5 mg/kg weekly (DailyMed setid 2483adba-fab6-4d1b-96c5-c195577ed071) that is a full year of prophylaxis for a patient of about 64 kg and roughly five-sevenths of one for a 90 kg adult, so the allowed amount is close to a true annual price here and the discontinuation rate below is not doing much work. Medicare is a small and old slice of a disease whose US population is mostly young and commercially insured - 438 Part B beneficiaries against a US hemophilia A population in the tens of thousands - so the per-beneficiary figure is a Medicare allowed amount rather than a national average net price

Lee JS, Schuldt R, Xia Z, Lee L, Biondo JML, Shapiro AD, 'Real-world adherence to and persistence with emicizumab in people with hemophilia A using a national claims database', J Manag Care Spec Pharm 2026;32(2):135-142, doi:10.18553/jmcp.2026.32.2.135, PMID 41636686: in 280 people with hemophilia A in IQVIA PharMetrics Plus over November 2017 to September 2023, 237 (84.6%) were persistent at 12 months, discontinuation being a gap of at least 60 days. 1 - 0.846 = 0.1536
column12: Cross-check from the other direction: the CMS Part B 2024 consumption of 5,003 mg per beneficiary against a labelled year at 1.5 mg/kg weekly implies 0.86 of a year on drug for a 75 kg patient and 0.71 for a 90 kg one, which brackets the claims figure. The claims study measures the first year after starting, when discontinuation is highest in most chronic therapies, so this may overstate the steady-state rate; against that, a 60-day gap is a loose definition that will miss patients who lapse and restart

column11: Soucie JM, Miller CH, Byams VR, Payne AB, Abe K, Sidonio RF Jr, Kouides PA, 'Occurrence rates of von Willebrand disease among people receiving care in specialized treatment centres in the United States', Haemophilia 2021;27(3):445-453, doi:10.1111/hae.14263, PMID 33780098, PMC10591267: 24,238 patients with von Willebrand disease were seen at US haemophilia treatment centres over 2012-2019, of whom 456 had type 3, and 'the overall HTC-treated prevalence of Type 2 was 1.2 cases per 100 K and that of Type 3 was 2 cases per million'. Applied to the 340,110,988 US residents of 1 July 2024 (Census): 2 per million x 340,110,988 = 680
column12: a lower bound, and twice over. It counts only people receiving care at a haemophilia treatment centre, and the same paper's age-adjusted table reads 0.2 cases per 100,000, which is the same figure to one significant digit. Type 3 is the severe form, with essentially absent von Willebrand factor and a bleeding phenotype that presents in infancy, so the share managed outside a treatment centre should be small - smaller than for types 1 and 2 - but it is not nil. No incidence row is written: type 3 is congenital and lifelong, so the pool is a stock, and no US incidence per live birth with a usable denominator was found in this session

column11: the layer's population is the descriptor itself. WILL-EMI (NCT06998524) enrols patients with confirmed type 3 von Willebrand disease from one month of age in three arms that between them cover the whole treated population: patients previously on intermittent on-demand therapy, randomised against continued on-demand standard of care, and patients previously on prophylaxis one to three times weekly. No sourced share narrows the pool further, and type 3 is by definition the severe form in which essentially all patients need treatment
column12: the requirement in the randomised arms of at least two treated bleeds in the 24 weeks before enrolment is a real restriction on the trial and is carried in the penetration peak below, because no US figure for the share of type 3 patients meeting it could be sourced

column1: ROG
column11: a judgement, and the row to argue with. The case for a high share: a subcutaneous injection every one to four weeks against intravenous von Willebrand factor concentrate infused one to three times a week is the same convenience argument that took emicizumab to the majority of US hemophilia A prophylaxis, and this would be the first non-factor prophylactic agent in type 3 disease. The case for a low one, which is why the number is not higher: emicizumab bridges factor IXa and factor X and so substitutes for factor VIII, but it does not replace von Willebrand factor, so it cannot correct the platelet adhesion defect that drives the mucocutaneous, gastrointestinal and menstrual bleeding type 3 patients suffer. Those patients would still need concentrate for that bleeding, which is a reason to prescribe emicizumab alongside rather than instead
